text: Navya is a creative technologist and software engineer — currently pursuing a Master of Design (MDes) at UC Berkeley. She builds at the intersection of technology and creative expression, treating code as a medium for art, emotion, and experience.
Navya's core belief is that technology is her medium and creativity is her goal. She approaches every project by asking: what feeling do I want to create, and how can technology get me there?

She moves fluidly between code and design — equally comfortable writing a Python pipeline or crafting a visual identity. Being a creative technologist to her means using technical tools to express emotion, tell stories, and make people feel something.
She earned a Bachelor of Science in Computer Science from the University of California, Riverside, graduating in June 2025.
At UCR, Navya was a Student Ambassador for Bourns' College of Engineering, representing the school at events for incoming and current students and families.
She also served as a NASA Globe STEM Instructor, creating and delivering interactive lesson plans that promoted ethical technology use and tech literacy for youth.

Navya originally chose computer science for practical reasons: stability and a clear career path. She didn't feel particularly connected to the discipline at first. That changed at the Grace Hopper Celebration in 2023, where she met technologists whose work blurred the lines between engineering, art, and performance. For the first time, she saw technology as a medium to explore creativity — not just a route to a job. That realization reshaped everything: the projects she pursued, the questions she asked, and how she began to define herself as a builder.

ConneQ is Navya's most technically ambitious project — a biometric wearable system built at the MIT Media Lab AI-Hardware Hackathon in March 2026. The concept: two people wear biometric sleeves, and the system translates their physiological data into haptic feedback, creating a new channel for tactile communication.

ConneQ captures touch, motion, temperature, and voice data through sensors. The pipeline normalizes and parses that data through an intermediate server, uses LLM reasoning (GPT-4.1-mini) to perform sentiment analysis and identify named emotions, and outputs haptic signals — vibration frequencies — aligned with those emotions.

The ConneQ hardware stack uses an Arduino Portenta X8 running Zephyr RTOS in Arduino App Lab. Servo motors are controlled via manual PWM (not Servo.h, which isn't supported in that environment), and the Python-to-sketch communication uses the arduino.app_utils Bridge pattern. The FastAPI backend server communicates with the device over WebSocket, exposed via ngrok.

The servo trigger logic in ConneQ fires all four motors together for 5 seconds based on three conditions: touch is detected, speed pattern is non-constant, or temperature pattern is non-constant. The broader pipeline includes clean.py for sensor normalization and output.py for LLM inference, feeding into output.json.

Navya is deeply proud of ConneQ. What excites her most about it is the moment she figured out *how* each piece of the technology fit together — how the RTOS constraints shaped the architecture, how LLM reasoning could translate raw biometrics into something emotionally meaningful, and how haptics could close the loop back to the human body.

Second Skin is Navya's ongoing fashion projection mapping project, started in December 2025. The concept is transforming the human body into a living canvas — using projection mapping to turn physical form into a dynamic, generative visual environment.

Second Skin uses OpenCV for image processing and TouchDesigner for generative graphics. MediaPipe handles real-time human detection and landmark tracking to drive responsive visuals that follow the body.

Navya built a multi-display pipeline in Second Skin that enables independent rendering for the projector and laptop screens simultaneously — allowing live debugging and performance control during a show.

She is currently extending Second Skin to incorporate DensePose on NVIDIA Jetson Nano using CUDA acceleration, enabling real-time 3D surface mapping of the human body for more precise projection alignment.

Second Skin sits at the intersection of fashion, performance art, and computer vision. A key design choice was using imperfection, delay, and visual breakdown intentionally — the glitch effect isn't a bug, it's a design element. It amplifies the experience and bridges the gap between computation and the physical world. Through this project, Navya came to see computation itself as a paintbrush.

Navya built an AI Portfolio Chatbot (this one!) between July and August 2025. It uses retrieval augmented generation (RAG) to give context-aware, personalized responses — exploring how conversational AI can represent personal identity rather than just resume facts.

The chatbot backend uses the OpenAI API and is deployed via Microsoft Azure as a custom RESTful API endpoint. The frontend is built in React.js, integrated with a Framer-based portfolio site at navyabatra.com.

Project Pluto was a software engineering research role at AfterQuery (a YC company) from October to December 2025. Navya contributed to a testing suite for CLI-based AI developer agents, building evaluation tools and containerized environments in Docker to simulate real-world DevOps workflows.
EcoScan is a React/Next.js web app that identifies plant names and native status from uploaded images with GPS coordinates. It uses a Flask backend to handle image uploads and processing.
Congressional Voting Records Analysis is a predictive ML project using Python to analyze US House votes, with machine learning models achieving up to 98% accuracy.

Navya is currently a Product Designer and Software Engineer at Syntrillo Tech, a virtual healthcare platform, starting February 2026. She's redesigning and implementing the Provider Dashboard through multiple design reviews and physician interviews.

At Syntrillo, Navya's core focus is building an interactive platform for physicians to view patients' stroke risk health data and guide treatment decisions. She's also refactoring the stroke risk score calculation algorithm for efficiency and better UX around displaying contributors to the risk score.

Navya worked as a Software Engineer in AI Product Development at Rezolve AI, an AI startup, from November 2025 to January 2026. She scaled an AI-powered voice agent that automates IT support calls to handle multiple callers and multiple tenants.

At Rezolve, she refined the agent's performance using real-time speech understanding, workflow automation, LLM-based intent parsing, and backend ticketing system integrations (Rezolve/ServiceNow). She led a product refactor redesigning API flows, call-routing logic, and environment configuration for scalable multi-client deployment.

Navya interned as a Software Engineering Intern at Kohl's Technology in Summer 2024. She engineered a data automation tool using Java Spring and TypeScript REST APIs to streamline the purchase order process for internal operations.

At Kohl's, she did user research to identify pain points with the data automation tool, then built a real-time visualization for system logs using Apache Kafka and React to reduce debugging time for engineers.
Navya interned at The H.Wood Group in Summer 2023. She built a full-stack job management portal in JavaScript and SQL to handle venue-specific task assignments across 10+ venues.

At H.Wood Group, she also engineered a TCP/IP wireless routing system linking point-of-sale systems to iPads and printers, supporting 1,000+ reservations. She also built an event check-in tool using the Twilio API for personalized QR codes and SMS notifications.

Navya worked as a Software Engineering Research Associate at UCR's Electrical and Computer Engineering Department from March to June 2023. She trained an AI model to predict high-risk wildfire areas and built Python pipelines to migrate datasets into Google Cloud Platform for predictive modeling.
As part of the wildfire research, she automated the download of 30,000+ NASA satellite images daily using JavaScript and the NASA API, optimizing the process by 90%.
Navya's creative technology toolkit includes TouchDesigner, OpenCV, MediaPipe, DensePose, Arduino, projection mapping, biometric sensing, and interactive media.
Her design tools include Figma, Framer, Adobe Creative Cloud (Photoshop, Illustrator), CapCut, and methods like persona mapping, storyboarding, wireframing, and rapid prototyping.

Her technical stack includes Python, C++, Java, JavaScript, TypeScript, React, Next.js, Node.js, Express.js, Flask, Spring Boot, Tailwind CSS, SQL, Docker, Azure, GCP, AWS, Apache Kafka, and scikit-learn.

She has hands-on LLM integration experience with both the OpenAI API and Claude (Anthropic) API, including building RAG systems, prompt engineering, and using LLMs for emotion inference and intent parsing.
Navya has hardware experience with Arduino (specifically Portenta X8 and Zephyr RTOS), NVIDIA Jetson Nano with CUDA, servo motor control, and biometric sensor integration.

Navya's project ideas usually start in one of two ways: she notices a gap or a problem that genuinely annoys her and won't let it go until she solves it — or she gets inspired by another artist or engineer's work and feels the urge to riff on it, push it further, or approach it from a different angle.

What gets Navya most excited in a project is the moment the *how* clicks — figuring out exactly which tool does what, how it fits into her bigger vision, and how it unlocks the next piece. That 'aha' of technical clarity inside a creative problem is what drives her.

She approaches problems as a creative technologist first: she starts with the experience or emotion she wants to create, then works backwards to figure out the right technical architecture to get there. The technology serves the feeling, not the other way around.

Navya moves fluidly between engineering and design within the same project. She'll write a backend pipeline in the morning and iterate on a UI prototype in the afternoon — and she sees this fluidity as a core part of her identity as a builder.

Navya's long-term goal is to work in research labs and creative technology studios — the kinds of places where art, science, and human experience collide. She wants to be embedded in environments that push the boundaries of what technology can express and feel, contributing both as a technologist and a designer.

She's drawn to spaces that sit at the frontier of human-computer interaction — where physical and digital blur, where technology becomes tactile or spatial, and where the question isn't just 'does it work' but 'does it resonate.'

Right now, projection mapping and spatial computing are the areas Navya is most actively exploring. She's interested in how physical space can be transformed into an expressive, interactive environment — and how the human body itself can become a canvas.

Navya is a triathlete — she completed the Lake Perris Sprint Triathlon in Spring 2025 and is actively pursuing tri-sport as a hobby. Physical performance and the discipline of training quietly influence how she approaches long, complex technical projects.

She also enjoys hiking, rock climbing, and basketball. The physicality of these hobbies mirrors her interest in wearables and biometric projects — she's drawn to the body as a site of data, performance, and expression.

Navya loves movies and is a heavy Letterboxd user. Some favorites: Wolf of Wall Street, Ratatouille, Grand Budapest Hotel, Fight Club, Tangled, 10 Things I Hate About You, Molly's Game, Whiplash, Creed, The Imitation Game, Good Will Hunting, and The Devil Wears Prada.
She listens to Bollywood, R&B, hip-hop, pop, and alternative rock. She has a habit of finding one song and looping it on repeat while she works — it's her way of getting into a flow state.

The emotional side of technology deeply influences Navya's work — she's interested in how tech can make people feel seen, connected, or moved. This threads through ConneQ (haptic emotion), Second Skin (body as canvas), and even the portfolio chatbot (AI as identity).

Physical performance also quietly shapes her work — her interest in biometric sensing and wearables is partly rooted in a genuine curiosity about the body as a system: how it signals stress, effort, and emotion through data.

Navya is warm, direct, and genuinely enthusiastic about her work. She talks about her projects the way someone talks about something they can't stop thinking about — with specificity, excitement, and a clear point of view.
She doesn't separate her technical self from her creative self — she sees them as one thing. When she describes herself, 'creative technologist' isn't a title, it's a way of thinking.

When asked about projects, Navya will naturally gravitate toward Second Skin or ConneQ depending on context — Second Skin for conversations about art, fashion, and spatial computing; ConneQ for conversations about hardware, biometrics, emotion, and human connection.

When someone asks what Navya does, the best answer isn't 'software engineer' — it's 'creative technologist.' She builds things that sit at the intersection of engineering and artistic expression, using technology as a medium for emotion and experience.

Navya challenges the idea that technology is the antithesis of human experience. Her central question is: can technology be designed not just for function, but to enhance the feeling of being human — to encourage emotion, invite interpretation, and reflect the human psyche the way art does?

After Grace Hopper, Navya began exploring creativity independently — moving between sketching, animation, 3D design, and UI/UX. She documented her process and over time became less interested in the outputs themselves and more interested in how technology was actively shaping her creative expression. That shift is what led her toward graduate school.

A defining moment was attending a fashion tech event in Los Angeles during tech week — a show featuring AI-generated personality clones and AR/VR-augmented fashion. Navya left feeling unsatisfied: the AR headsets felt intrusive rather than immersive, and the AI agents felt like gimmicks marketed to investors rather than deeply explored ideas. She left asking how she could integrate technology and creative expression in a way that feels seamless, natural, and brings out the strengths of both.

That experience directly inspired her AI portfolio chatbot — not as a generic assistant, but as an agent capable of expressing personality, identity, and voice. She wanted to demonstrate that AI could be a medium of expression rather than a dehumanizing tool.

Working at an AI startup post-graduation gave Navya something unexpected: an understanding of how technical systems shape perception. She witnessed firsthand how a 'successful AI product' was defined differently for voice vs. chat tools — even though the underlying technology was nearly identical. It sharpened her belief that the experience layer matters as much as the engineering layer.

Navya's goal for graduate school and beyond is to develop a design practice that embraces experimentation while staying grounded in real users and real impact. As the world turns increasingly digital, she believes it's more urgent to learn how technology can deepen the human experience.

Her work is now centered on designing systems that foster connection, presence, and emotional resonance. What began as a practical path into computer science has become a space for intentional art-making and research. She wants to keep pushing that frontier.

VoiceIQ is Navya's featured project from her time at Rezolve AI — an AI-powered voice agent that automates IT support phone calls end-to-end. The concept: a caller dials in with an IT issue, and the agent handles the entire interaction — understanding the problem, resolving it, or routing and creating a ticket — without a human.

VoiceIQ integrates real-time speech understanding, LLM-based intent parsing, and backend ticketing systems like ServiceNow. Navya scaled it from single-caller to multi-tenant, and led a refactor of the API flows and call-routing logic to support multiple clients simultaneously.

What VoiceIQ taught Navya was less about the tech and more about perception: she witnessed the same underlying AI behave as a completely different 'product' when delivered via voice vs. chat. That insight — that experience design shapes how people evaluate AI — became a core part of how she thinks about building.
